clue.text: One of the skills of Berlioz (The Corsair not in this arrangement)

definitions.text: One of the skills of Berlioz
definitions.note: Berlioz wrote a famous treatise on scoring for instruments, and an overture called Le Corsaire

indicators.note: an arrangement reorders things, so the bracketed words are to be set out in a new order

explanation.surface: A remark on a Berlioz overture, The Corsair, said to be missing from some musical arrangement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in this arrangement' shuffles THE CORSAIR NOT; the bracket hides the fact that the overture title is the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Scoring music for the instruments of an orchestra was a skill Berlioz was renowned for and wrote a treatise on.

clue.text: Climber and walker in the country()

explanation.surface: A person who climbs mountains and hikes through the countryside.
explanation.definitionFit: A rambling rose is a climbing plant, and a hiker strolling through the countryside is one who rambles.

clue.text: Passion aroused in division of race

explanation.surface: A runner's emotions run high during one round of a race.
explanation.definitionFit: Strong roused feeling is ardour, and a preliminary round of a race is one of its qualifying stages.

clue.text: Shaken cider as a type of cocktail

indicators.note: shaking a drink mixes it up, so the letters of these words are jumbled

explanation.surface: A barman shakes cider to make a cocktail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shaken' belongs to cocktail-making in the surface, but it shuffles CIDER AS.
explanation.definitionFit: The sidecar is a classic mixed drink of brandy, orange liqueur and lemon juice.

clue.text: Uneasy sleep I have to follow

parts.note: rest is a synonym for sleep
I have shortens to I've, written without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone restless knows they will have to sleep next.
explanation.walkthrough: The page drops the 'I' before 'have'; the wordplay needs 'I have', contracted to I'VE, which simply follows REST.
explanation.definitionFit: Restive describes someone fidgety and unable to settle, which is to be ill at ease.

clue.text: Fashion for a short walk

explanation.surface: Clothing style suitable for a brief stroll.
explanation.definitionFit: To fashion something on a lathe is to shape it that way, and taking a brief stroll is going for one.

clue.text: Hard rock endlessly, perhaps, in Granny Smith's garden

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters might be put another way, so they are rearranged
without its end, the word rock loses its final letter

explanation.surface: Solid rock everywhere in an old woman's garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' cuts ROCK to ROC; 'perhaps' then shuffles HARD plus ROC. Granny Smith is an apple variety, so her garden is where apple trees grow.
explanation.definitionFit: A Granny Smith is a variety of apple, and the place where apple trees are grown is a fruit garden.

clue.text: Fly Pop over tedious flight stages

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece over another means it sits above it, so it comes first

parts.note: pop is an informal word for father
long can mean tedious, as in a long day
the legs of a journey are its stages

explanation.surface: Dad covers a boring flight with several stops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fly' looks like a verb about air travel but is the insect, the crane fly.
explanation.definitionFit: The crane fly, a long-legged insect, is known by this nickname in Britain.

clue.text: Tom, a sub normal sort of kipper!

definitions.note: one who kips, that is sleeps, the noun from slang 'kip'

indicators.note: a sort of something is a variant of it, so these letters are reworked

explanation.surface: An insult calling Tom a rather dim sort of smoked fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' shuffles TOM A SUB NORMAL. A kipper is a smoked herring, but here it is one who kips (sleeps).
explanation.definitionFit: A sleepwalker is a person who walks while asleep, so a sleeper of a particular type.

clue.text: A jolly group of players displayed on the sleeve

parts.note: a jolly is old slang for a Royal Marine, abbreviated RM
a band is a group of musicians

explanation.surface: A cheerful group of musicians wears something on their sleeves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jolly' looks like an adjective but is the noun: a Royal Marine (RM).
explanation.definitionFit: A band of cloth is worn round the upper arm to show office or mourning.

clue.text: Wind up in the desert

parts.note: a hot wind that rises in the Sahara and blows north across the Mediterranean

explanation.surface: Someone finishing their journey somewhere in the desert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wind up' reads as 'end up', but it is a wind that gets up in the Sahara.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the hot dusty wind that blows from North Africa, originating over the Sahara.

clue.text: Puppet of old-fashioned length

indicators.note: fashioned means made into a new shape, so the word old is rearranged

explanation.surface: A puppet from an antique, long-gone era.
explanation.walkthrough: 'old-fashioned' looks like one adjective, but 'fashioned' shuffles OLD into DOL.
explanation.definitionFit: A doll is a toy figure, and a person controlled by another may be called one, like a puppet.

clue.text: Small piece of paper scenario has to be cut short

indicators.note: trimming the word short drops its last letter

parts.note: a scenario is a film script

explanation.surface: A film outline must be shortened to fit on a scrap of paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut short' takes the T off SCRIPT.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrip is a certificate or slip of paper, such as one given to shareholders.

clue.text: High water for Jack Point

parts.note: a jack tar is a sailor, so jack gives tar
N is a point of the compass, north

explanation.surface: A reference to Jack Point, the jester in Gilbert and Sullivan's The Yeomen of the Guard.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack Point looks like one name, but split it: Jack is a sailor (TAR) and Point a compass point (N).
explanation.definitionFit: A small mountain lake lies high up in hills, so it is water at altitude.

clue.text: Black mark for this slanderous attack

explanation.surface: A stain on someone's name is grounds for a libel suit.
explanation.definitionFit: A dirty streak is a stain, and an untrue accusation meant to damage a reputation is a slur.

clue.text: Fellow gets title in Open

parts.note: a rank, such as colonel, is a title of standing

explanation.surface: A man wins a championship title at a golf or tennis Open.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Open' looks like a tournament, but it is the adjective meaning candid.
explanation.definitionFit: Being candid and plain-spoken is the same as being open with people.

clue.text: One hopes to make a good bit at work

definitions.text: One hopes to make a good bit at work

parts.words: One hopes to make a good bit at work
parts.note: a craftsman whose job is making metal mouthpieces for horses' bridles, along with spurs and stirrups

explanation.surface: A worker hoping to earn a decent amount on the job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a good bit' suggests money; it is the metal bit in a horse's mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: A lorimer was a maker of bits, spurs and other metal parts of a horse's harness.

clue.text: Lord's ground?

parts.note: the lands or domain held by a nobleman of a certain rank

explanation.surface: A question about Lord's, the London cricket ground.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord's is the famous London cricket ground, but here a lord's territory is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: The territory ruled by a nobleman of this rank is his domain, his estate.

clue.text: Fresh approach to Old Nick

parts.note: new means fresh
a gate is the approach or entrance to a place

explanation.surface: A new way of handling the Devil.
explanation.walkthrough: Old Nick is a name for the Devil, but 'nick' is British slang for prison: Newgate was London's old prison.
explanation.definitionFit: Newgate was a notorious London jail, and 'nick' is British slang for a prison.

clue.text: Brave signals unit?

parts.note: a Native American warrior (a brave) sends signals with this percussion instrument

explanation.surface: An army regiment that handles communications, praised for courage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'signals unit' suggests a military corps; 'Brave' is a Native American warrior who signals with a drum.
explanation.definitionFit: A drum beaten to call warriors to battle or send signals between them.

clue.text: One who throws out a seat

definitions.text: One who throws out a seat

parts.words: One who throws out a seat
parts.note: a bouncer who ejects people, and also the word paired with seat for a pilot's escape chair

explanation.surface: A bouncer removing a chair, or a person.
explanation.definitionFit: An ejector expels things, and in aircraft an ejector seat throws out the pilot.

clue.text: Kicking Anne out means the boot

indicators.note: kicking things about scatters them, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Throwing Anne out means giving her the boot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the boot' looks like dismissal; it is the rear part of a car, the tonneau. 'Kicking' shuffles ANNE OUT.
explanation.definitionFit: The tonneau is the rear passenger section of an old open car, behind the front seats.

clue.text: Proverbially thick-set?

parts.note: the group named in the saying 'as thick as ...' for close friends

explanation.surface: Asking whether someone is stockily built, as the saying goes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thick-set' reads as burly, but it is the set that is proverbially thick: 'thick as thieves'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'as thick as thieves' describes people who are very close, so the robbers form the thick set.

clue.text: Wearing down or, in row, rising

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means read from the bottom up, so the whole is reversed
or is placed inside the word for row

parts.note: a row is a din, a noise
taken as written

explanation.surface: A disagreement about wearing things out, in a row that grows heated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts OR into NOISE, giving NOISORE; 'rising' turns it upwards to read EROSION.
explanation.definitionFit: Erosion is the gradual wearing away of rock or soil by wind and water.

clue.text: Frolic long longboat of old

parts.note: Noah's ark is the ancient boat

explanation.surface: Playful fun in a Viking longboat of times past.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints 'longboat'; the wordplay needs 'long boat' as two words: L (long) and ARK.
explanation.definitionFit: A lark is a bit of fun or a prank, a frolic.

clue.text: Mince pies a brown colour in the main

definitions.note: a brown pigment from the ink of a sea creature; the main is the sea

indicators.note: mincing chops things up, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Mince pies baked to a brown colour, mainly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mince pies' looks like the Christmas treat, but 'Mince' shuffles PIES A. 'the main' is the sea: sepia is the cuttlefish whose ink gives the colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Sepia is a reddish-brown pigment made from cuttlefish ink, a creature of the sea.

clue.text: It reduces the spirits!

parts.note: a mixer added to whisky or brandy waters down its strength

explanation.surface: Something that dampens one's mood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reduces the spirits' sounds like depressing someone; it is diluting liquor, as in whisky and soda.
explanation.definitionFit: Fizzy water is added to whisky to dilute the alcohol.

clue.text: Girl getting rave review

indicators.note: to review is to look at again, signalling the letters are reordered

explanation.surface: A young woman's show gets glowing praise from critics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rave review' looks like praise, but 'review' shuffles RAVE.
explanation.definitionFit: Vera is a woman's given name.

clue.text: For the bowler's part, bowled Border!

parts.note: B is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for bowled
a rim is a border or edge

explanation.surface: A cricket commentary: as for the bowler, he bowled out Border, the Australian batsman.
explanation.walkthrough: Allan Border was an Australian cricket captain, and the bowler a cricketer; here a bowler is a hat, whose edge is its brim.
explanation.definitionFit: A bowler hat has a curled edge round its crown that is one of its parts.

clue.text: MN great-coat, for example

annotationWithheld.why: 'MN great-coat, for example' (7): GARMENT is an anagram of MN GREAT but no clue word signals the anagram, and 'great' cannot be both fodder and indicator

clue.text: Green, I turn, suffering from it

definitions.text: Green, I turn, suffering from it

parts.note: vert is the heraldic word for green
a go is a turn, as in 'your go'

explanation.surface: A dizzy sufferer feels green and as if spinning round.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: someone with this condition feels green and that they are turning.
explanation.definitionFit: Vertigo is the dizziness that makes the world seem to spin and leaves sufferers feeling sick.

clue.text: Barman's terms a possible cause of money trouble

indicators.note: a cause of something produces it, and 'possible' marks one of many ways the letters could be worked into a new form

parts.note: the printed words, whose final A should have been an E for the letters to match

explanation.surface: A barman's prices could lead to running short of cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possible cause of' shuffles BARMAN'S TERMS A, but those letters hold three As and one E; the answer needs two of each, so the setter's A should be an E.
explanation.definitionFit: Financial embarrassment is a polite term for being short of money.
